en: Vasubandhu: Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only.
Homage to the Buddha.

The *Triṃśikāvijñaptiprakaraṇa* is commenced for the purpose of demonstrating the non-perverted selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*) and phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) to those who have not realized or have wrongly realized these two. Furthermore, the demonstration of the selflessness of persons and phenomena is for the sake of abandoning the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). For it is from the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) that the afflictions such as attachment arise; and since the realization of the selflessness of persons is the antidote to the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), when it proceeds toward the abandonment of that [view], it abandons all afflictions.
One abandons [them];

furthermore, because the knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) serves as the antidote to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the cognitive obscurations are abandoned.
Moreover, the abandonment of both the afflictive and cognitive obscurations is for the sake of attaining liberation and omniscience.
For the afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed an obstruction to the attainment of liberation; therefore, when they are abandoned, liberation is realized.
The obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is likewise undefiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*), which acts as a hindrance to the operation of knowledge regarding all that is to be known.
When that is abandoned, knowledge proceeds unhindered and unimpeded with respect to all aspects of the knowable; thus, omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is attained.

Alternatively, because those who are attached to phenomena (dharma) and persons (pudgala) do not know that there is mind-only (cittamātra) as it truly is, this treatise is commenced in order to lead them, by means of demonstrating the selflessness of phenomena and persons, into the state of representation-only (vijñaptimātra) along with its fruit in a gradual manner. Alternatively, some believe that just like consciousness, the object of cognition (vijñeya) also exists substantially (dravyataḥ).
The commencement of this treatise is for the purpose of refuting both these types of extremist views—that consciousness, like the object of cognition, exists only conventionally and not ultimately.
The various metaphorical designations (*upacāra*) of self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) that occur—
in both the world and in treatises— is [actually] in the transformation of consciousness (*vijñānapariṇāma*). This is the completion of the sentence.
The phrase "the metaphorical designation of self and phenomena" (ātmadharmopacāra) is connected [to the preceding].
Since the self and phenomena are metaphorically designated, it is called the "metaphorical designation of self and phenomena.
Furthermore, that consists of the conceptual designation of a self and the conceptual designation of phenomena.
"Various" means of many kinds.

The metaphorical designation of a self (*ātman*)—such as "living being," "creature," "human," or "mortal"—is the metaphorical designation of a self. The metaphorical designation of phenomena (*dharma*)—such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—is the metaphorical designation of phenomena.
Both of these two types of metaphorical designation are merely the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*); they do not exist in a primary sense within a self or within phenomena.
Why is this so?
Because phenomena and the self do not exist externally apart from the transformation of consciousness.
What, then, is this so-called "transformation"?

Alteration (*anyathātva*) is the acquisition of its own nature by the effect, which occurs simultaneously with the cessation of the causal moment and is distinct from that causal moment; this is transformation (*pariṇāma*).

In this regard, due to the nourishment of the latencies (*vāsanā*) for the conceptualization of a self and so forth, and due to the nourishment of the latencies for the conceptualization of form and so forth, there arises from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) a conceptualization manifesting as a self and so forth, as well as a conceptualization manifesting as form and so forth.

Based upon that appearance of a self and so forth, and the appearance of form and so forth— which, though not existing externally to that conceptual construction— there proceeds from beginningless time the metaphorical designation of a self and the metaphorical designation of phenomena such as form,
even in the absence of any external self or phenomena.
It is just like the metaphorical designation of a mass of hair and so forth for one suffering from ophthalmia.
And when something does not exist in a certain place, it is applied there figuratively;
for example, "cow" in reference to a *bāhīka*.

Likewise, because the self (*ātman*) and its phenomena (*dharma*) do not exist either in the nature of consciousness or externally, the self and phenomena are merely imagined (*parikalpita*) and do not exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). Thus, just like consciousness, the object of cognition (*vijñeya*) also exists as a substantial reality (*dravyataḥ*).
This extremist position is not to be accepted.

Since a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) cannot exist without a basis, one must necessarily admit that the transformation of consciousness (*vijñānapariṇāma*) exists in reality—that is, as a factual entity—upon which the metaphorical designations of self and phenomena proceed.

Therefore, this further admission is not tenable by reasoning: namely, that consciousness, like the object of cognition, exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛti*) and not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

"Because it would follow that even conventionally there is non-existence—for a convention without a basis is not tenable—therefore this one-sided doctrine, in both its forms, must be abandoned due to its lack of logical justification; such is the statement of the Master (Ācārya).

And thus, it should be accepted that all objects of cognition do not exist in reality because they are of an imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), whereas consciousness, on the other hand, exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*) because it is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*)."
Furthermore, the fact that consciousness is dependently originated is indicated by the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
How is it understood that consciousness itself arises bearing the form of an object without an external object?

For an external object is accepted as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of consciousness by virtue of its producing a consciousness that bears its own appearance, and not merely by being a cause; otherwise, there would be no distinction from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and other such conditions.
Furthermore, the five groups of consciousness have accumulated objects as their focal points because they possess the aspect of those [objects].
And an accumulation does not exist apart from the mere collection of parts;
for once those parts are excluded, there is no cognition possessing the aspect of an accumulation.
Therefore, consciousness arises with an aggregated form even without an external object.
Nor are the atoms themselves, when aggregated, its objective support (*ālambana*), because atoms do not possess that [aggregated] form.
For there is no specific excellence in the nature of the atoms in their aggregated state that was not already present in their non-aggregated state.
Therefore, atoms, whether unaggregated or aggregated, are not at all an object of cognition.
However, another [teacher] thinks:
"A single atom, independent of others, is beyond the senses; but many [atoms], depending upon one another, are graspable by the senses."

For these [atoms] as well, since there is no excellence of their own nature (*ātmaniṣeṣa*) in either the dependent or independent state, they must be either exclusively perceptible by the senses or entirely beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

Furthermore, if atoms themselves, in mutual dependence, become the objects of consciousness, then this distinction of forms such as jars, walls, and so forth, which appears in consciousness, would not exist; for atoms do not possess those forms.
Furthermore, it is not logical for a consciousness that appears as one thing to have an object that has a different form, because that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Nor do atoms exist in an ultimate sense, like pillars and other objects,
because they possess near, middle, and far parts.
Alternatively, if that [spatial extension] is not admitted, then the distinctions of direction—east, south, west, north, and so forth—which belong to the atom, would not exist.
Consequently, it follows that the atom, like consciousness, would be formless and devoid of spatial location.
Thus, one must accept that because external objects do not exist, consciousness itself arises in the form of an object, just like a dream-consciousness.
Feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] likewise do not produce consciousness with their own aspects when they are past or future, because they have already ceased or have not yet arisen.
Nor do they produce it when present, because they are non-existent during the state of being in the process of arising (*utpadyamānāvasthā*).

When they have reached the state of having arisen, since consciousness has also already arisen with that aspect, there is nothing further to be done; thus, even mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises without an object (*anālambana*).
But another says:
"If a primary self did not exist, and if [primary] phenomena did not exist, metaphorical designation would not be tenable.

For metaphorical designation occurs when three things are present, and not in the absence of any one of them: a primary referent, another object that resembles it, and the similarity between the two."

For example, when there is a primary fire and a boy resembling it, and when there exists a common property between the two—such as being tawny or being sharp—the metaphorical designation "the boy is fire" is employed.
For in this case, either a genus (*jāti*) or a substance (*dravya*) is being metaphorically attributed in the expression "the boy is fire.
In both instances, however, there is an absence of metaphorical application.
In that case, first of all, neither tawny color nor sharpness is common to the genus [of fire].
And in the absence of a common property, it is not logical to apply the designation of the genus to the boy (māṇavaka), because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Even if the genus does not possess those properties, as regards sharpness and tawny color—
It might be argued that because [sharpness] is invariably concomitant with the universal [of fire], there will be a metaphorical application of the universal to the boy (*māṇavaka*).
However, this invariable concomitance is untenable, because sharpness and tawny color are observed in the boy even in the absence of the universal.
Furthermore, if there were invariable concomitance, there would be no metaphorical usage, since the universal would actually exist in the boy just as it does in fire.
Therefore, a metaphorical application of the genus (*jāti*) to the boy is not possible;
nor is there a metaphorical application of the substance (*dravya*), because of the absence of common properties (*sāmānyadharma*).
For that quality which belongs to fire—whether it be sharpness or tawny color—is not the very same as that which belongs to the boy.
What then? It is something other than that.
Since a specific quality is dependent upon its own substratum, it is not logical to apply the metaphorical designation "fire" to a young boy in the absence of the quality of fire.
If it is argued that this is logical because of the similarity to the quality of fire, [we reply: no.

Even so, while a metaphorical application based on similarity is appropriate when the quality of fire—such as sharpness or tawny color—is applied to the qualities of a young brahmin boy, namely his sharpness or tawny color, it is not appropriate to apply it to the boy himself; for there is no connection [between the boy and the fire] by way of similarity of qualities.
Therefore, even a metaphorical application to the substance (dravya) is not tenable.
Furthermore, a primary referent (mukhya-padārtha) does not exist at all, because its own nature transcends the scope of all cognition and verbal designation.
For cognition and verbal designation operate with respect to the primary object only by way of its qualities, since they do not touch upon its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of the qualities being purposeless.

Indeed, there exists no other means for determining the essential nature of an entity apart from cognition and verbal designation; therefore, because of the absence of cognition and verbal designation directed toward the essential nature of the primary object, the primary object itself is not [directly apprehended].
Thus it should be understood.

In this way, up to the case of sound (*śabda*), because there is no relationship [between them], there is an absence of both cognition and designation; and since there is thus an absence of both designator and designated, there is no such thing as a primary category (*padārtha*).
Furthermore, all of this is merely figurative (*gauṇa*); there is nothing that is primary.
For that which functions by means of a form not present in its primary object is indeed called secondary (gauṇa).

And every word functions toward its primary object precisely by means of a form consisting of qualities (guṇa) that is not [inherently] present there; therefore, a primary [denotation] does not exist at all.
Thus, what was said—that if a self (ātman) does not exist as a primary [referent], figurative usage (upacāra) regarding phenomena (dharma) is not tenable—is incorrect.
It is not known how many divisions there are of the transformation of consciousness;
therefore, in order to demonstrate those divisions, he says:
"And that transformation is threefold. (1d)

That wherein there is the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of a self (*ātman*) and so forth, as well as the metaphorical designation of phenomena (*dharma*), is further divided into the state of cause and the state of fruit.

Among these, the transformation of the cause (*hetu-pariṇāma*) is the nourishment of the latencies of maturation (*vipāka-vāsanā*) and outflow (*niṣyanda-vāsanā*) within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The transformation of the fruit (*phala-pariṇāma*), moreover, is the manifestation in other homogeneous classes of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) upon the exhaustion of the projection of previous karma, due to the storehouse consciousness attaining the activity of the latencies of maturation.

Furthermore, due to the attainment of the activity of the outflowing latencies (*niṣyanda-vāsanā*), there occurs the manifestation of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) from the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
In this process, the evolving consciousness—whether wholesome or unwholesome—deposits both ripening latencies (*vipāka-vāsanā*) and outflowing latencies within the storehouse consciousness;
whereas the neutral and afflicted minds deposit only outflowing latencies.
That threefold transformation which has been mentioned is not yet understood;
therefore, in order to demonstrate its divisions, he says: "Maturation, that which is called mentation, and the representation of objects. (2ab)
Thus, this threefold transformation consists of that called maturation (*vipāka*), that called mentation (*manana*), and that called the representation of objects (*viṣayavijñapti*).
Among these, maturation is the production of a fruit according to its projection, by virtue of the ripening of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is always termed "mentation" because its essential nature is constant cogitation.

Because they manifest as objects such as visible form, the sixfold consciousnesses of the eye and so forth are the representation of objects (*viṣayavijñapti*). Since this [consciousness] cannot be understood without a description of its essential nature, the author, demonstrating the essential nature of each in due order, says:
"Therein, the consciousness called *ālaya* is the maturation (*vipāka*), containing all seeds" (2cd).
Thus [it is said]. "Therein" refers to this threefold transformation just mentioned.
That consciousness which is called "ālaya"—that is, designated as the *ālayavijñāna*—is the transformation of maturation (*vipāka-pariṇāma*).
And it is called "ālaya" because it is the locus for the seeds of all defiled phenomena (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*).

*Ālaya* and *sthāna* (abode) are synonyms. Alternatively, it is called *ālaya* because all phenomena (*dharma*) adhere to and are bound within it as effects, or because it adheres to and is bound within all phenomena as their cause.
It is called *vijñāna* (consciousness) because it cognizes.
It is called "maturation" (*vipāka*) because it is the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma within all realms, destinies, wombs, and births.
It is called "possessing all seeds" (*sarvabījaka*) because it is the substratum for the seeds of all phenomena.
If the *ālayavijñāna* exists as something distinct from the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), then its object (*ālambana*) or its mental aspect (*ākāra*) must be stated.
For it is not tenable that consciousness is without an object (*nirālambana*) or without an aspect (*nirākāra*).
Nor indeed is it accepted as being without an object or without an aspect;
rather, its object and aspect are undiscerned (*aparicchinna*).
What is the reason?
Because the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) functions in two ways:
internally as the representation of appropriation (upādāna-vijñapti), and externally as the representation of the environment (bhājana-vijñapti) in its undivided form.

In that context, internal appropriation consists of the latencies of the attachment to the imagined nature, along with the physical sense faculties together with their bases, and the mental factors (nāma).
Because this objective support is extremely subtle, it is characterized by an appropriation and a representation of its locus that are not consciously perceived. (3ab)

That in which appropriation (*upādi*) is not consciously perceived, and in which the representation of the locus (*sthāna-vijñapti*) is not consciously perceived, is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) characterized by the non-conscious perception of appropriation and the locus.
Appropriation (*upādi*) means grasping (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, that consists of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the conceptualization of a self and so forth, and the latencies of the conceptualization of phenomena such as form and so forth.

Because of its existence, the conceptualization of a self and so forth, as well as the conceptualization of form and so forth, are taken up by the *ālayavijñāna* as effects; therefore, it is called the "appropriation" (*upādi*) of those latencies consisting of the conceptualizations of a self and so forth, and the conceptualizations of form and so forth.
It is called "the appropriation that is not fully conscious" (*asaṃviditakopādi*) because it is not experienced in this [ālayavijñāna] through the mode of perceiving "this is that" or "that is this.
Furthermore, appropriation is the appropriation of the basis (*āśrayopādāna*).
The basis (*āśraya*) is the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), consisting of the material sense-faculties together with their foundations and the mental factors (*nāma*).
Furthermore, that which is its appropriation (*upādāna*)—its grasping [of these] as having a single security and well-being (*ekayogakṣematvena*)—is "that which is appropriated" (*upādi*).
In this regard, in the realms of desire and form, there is the appropriation of both name and form.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), however, because one is free from passion for form (*rūpavītarāgatva*) and thus there is no production of the maturation (*vipāka*) of form, there is only the appropriation of name (*nāmopādāna*).
Yet, form exists there only in the state of latent predisposition (*vāsanāvastha*) and not in the state of maturation.
Furthermore, because that appropriation cannot be experienced as "this," it is called "unperceived" (*asaṃvidita*).
The representation of place is the representation of the arrangement of the receptacle world.
That, too, is said to be "unconscious" because it functions with an object and aspect that are not clearly delimited.
How can consciousness have an object and aspect that are not clearly delimited?
This [objection] applies equally even to those who maintain that consciousness exists in other states;
for it cannot be established that consciousness does not exist at all during states such as the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
because that would contradict both reasoning and the sūtras.

In that regard, it has been stated that "the consciousness called *ālaya* (2c)" exists; and since consciousness is necessarily associated with mental factors (*caitta*), it must therefore be explained: with which ones and how many of them is it associated?
Likewise, is it always associated with them?
To this he says:

"It is always accompanied by contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition" (3cd). "Always" means that as long as the *ālayavijñāna* exists, it is accompanied by these five omnipresent factors (*sarvatraga-dharma*) known as contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition. Feeling is "experience" (*vit*).
In that context, contact (*sparśa*) is the discernment of the modification of the sense faculty when there is a conjunction of the three.
Its function is to provide a basis for feeling (*vedanā*).
The "triad" (*trika*) consists precisely of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
The simultaneous presence of these three in a relationship of cause and effect is the "coming together of the triad" (*trikasamnipāta*).

When that exists, at that very same time, there occurs a determination of the aspect of the object as being conducive to pleasant or other sensations; this determination, which corresponds to the modification of the sense faculty that is favorable toward sensations such as pleasure, is "contact" (*sparśa*).
Furthermore, the "modification" of the sense faculty is that specific quality by which it becomes the cause of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Furthermore, contact (*sparśa*) is so called because it touches the sense faculty by way of resembling a modification of that faculty, or because it is touched by the sense faculty;
for this very reason, although its nature consists in the discernment of the modification of the object, it is described as the discernment of the modification of the sense faculty.
Its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*).
For it is thus said in the Sūtra: "Dependent upon contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises," and so forth in detail.
Mental attention (*manaskāra*) is the application of the mind;
application is the act of applying.
It is that by which the mind is directed toward an object;
furthermore, its function is to maintain the mind upon that object.
Maintaining the mind, moreover, is the repeated application of the mind to that very same object.

And this [definition of] karma is stated with reference to a specific mental attention (*manaskāra*) characterized by the restriction of the object (*ālambana-niyama*) within the continuum of consciousness; it does not refer to that which occurs in every single moment of mind, for its activity pertains only to that very moment and not to another moment. Feeling (*vedanā*) has the nature of experience (*anubhava*).
Furthermore, that [feeling] is of three kinds, distinguished by the direct realization of the object's nature as being pleasant, painful, or distinct from both:
pleasant, painful, and neutral.
And it is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Others, however, think as follows:
"Experience" (anubhava) is that by which one experiences the ripening of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
In that regard, the ripening of the fruit of wholesome karmas is a pleasant experience; that of unwholesome karmas is painful;
and that of both is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
In this context, it is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) alone that is the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma;
and the equanimity associated with it is, in the ultimate sense, the fruition of those wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
As for pleasure and pain, they are metaphorically designated as "fruition" because they arise from the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
In this context, a pleasant experience (*sukha-anubhava*) is that which, when it has arisen, gives rise to a desire for non-separation, and when it has ceased, gives rise to a desire for reunion.
A painful experience (*duḥkha-anubhava*) is that which, when it has arisen, gives rise to a desire for separation, and when it has ceased, gives rise to a desire for non-reunion.
A neither-painful-nor-pleasant experience (*aduḥkhāsukha*) is that which, when it has arisen or ceased, neither of these two desires arises.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the grasping of the signs (*nimitta*) of objects (*viṣaya*).
An object is the focal point (*ālambana*).
A sign is its specific quality, the cause for establishing the focal point as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Its apprehension (*udgrahaṇa*) is its discernment (*nirūpaṇa*), such as "this is blue, not yellow.

Volition (*cetanā*) is the mental formation (*cittābhisaṃskāra*), the activity of the mind; when it exists, there occurs, as it were, a movement of the mind toward the object, like the movement of iron by the power of a magnet.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is threefold: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

There are four types of phenomena (*dharma*): wholesome, unwholesome, non-obscured neutral, and obscured neutral. In that regard, since it is not understood which of the three feelings (*vedanā*) is present in the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) based on the general teaching that "it is accompanied by feeling" (*savid*), and likewise because it is not understood whether it is wholesome, unwholesome, non-obscured neutral, or obscured neutral, he says:
Therein, the feeling is equanimity, and it is unobscured-neutral.
(4ab) The word "therein" refers specifically to the *ālayavijñāna*, as that is the subject under discussion.

In the *ālayavijñāna*, the feeling is exclusively equanimity—neither pleasure nor pain—because pleasure and pain have a distinct mode of apprehension regarding their objects and because they are accompanied by the latent tendencies of attachment and aversion.
And it is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
"The storehouse-consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*) is the subject under discussion.
In this context, the inclusion of the term "unobscured" (*anivṛta*) is for the purpose of excluding that which is obscured (*nivṛta*).
The inclusion of the term "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) is for the purpose of excluding the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*).
It is "unobstructed" (*anivṛta*) because it is not covered by adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) belonging to the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmika*).
It is "indeterminate" because, being a maturation (*vipāka*), it cannot be defined as either wholesome or unwholesome with respect to further maturation.
The same applies to contact (*sparśa*) and the others.
Just as the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is exclusively a maturation (*vipāka*), has an indistinct object and aspect, is always accompanied by contact and the other [mental factors],

and in that regard its feeling is exclusively equanimity (*upekṣā*) and it is non-defined (*avyākṛta*), so too contact and the others are exclusively maturations and have indistinct objects and aspects.

Excluding the self, these [mental factors] are always accompanied by the other four [universal factors] and by the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); and among them, feeling is exclusively equanimity. Like the storehouse consciousness, they are neutral (*avyākṛta*). For it is not possible for those associated with maturation (*vipāka*) to be non-maturation, nor for those with undiscerned objects and aspects to have discerned objects and aspects.
The same should be stated for other cases as well.
Furthermore, does that storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) persist as a single, undivided entity throughout the duration of saṃsāra,
or does it persist by way of a continuum? It does not persist as a single, undivided entity, because it is momentary (kṣaṇika).
What then?
And that proceeds like the current of a stream.
(4d) The word "that" refers specifically to the *ālayavijñāna*.
In this context, "stream" (*srotas*) refers to the continuous, uninterrupted progression of cause and effect.
Just as a current (*ogha*) is called a "flood" because it flows as a mass of water without interruption between its preceding and succeeding parts,

so too does the *ālayavijñāna* proceed, accompanied by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable karma, just as a flood moves along while dragging along grass, wood, cow dung, and the like.

"Drawing along contact, mental attention, and so forth, it proceeds without interruption through the stream of saṃsāra. To the question, "In what state does that which thus proceeds by way of a stream cease? he says:
"Its cessation occurs in Arhatship. (5a)
What, then, is arhatship?
By virtue of what is one called an "Arhat"?
Furthermore, by virtue of what is one called an "Arhat"?
This is because of the attainment of the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
For in that state, due to the abandonment without remainder of the dysfunctions (dauṣṭhulya) based upon the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the storehouse consciousness is overturned;
and that very state is the stage of an Arhat.
The transformation consisting of maturation has been explained with its detailed analysis.
Now, he describes the second transformation, called "mentation," with the words:
"It proceeds depending upon that," and so forth.

In this regard, just as the eyes and so forth are well known as the supports (*āśraya*) for the visual and other consciousnesses, and forms and so forth are well known as their objects (*ālambana*), neither the support nor the object of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is well known.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a consciousness to exist independently of a support and an object; therefore, in order to demonstrate the support and object of the afflicted mind, and in order to provide its etymological explanation (*nirukti*), he says:
"It proceeds by depending upon that."

The consciousness called *manas*, which has that as its object and consists of mentation (5bcd)—the word "that" in the phrase "arising in dependence on that" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*. For the *ālayavijñāna* is the locus of its latencies; therefore, "arising in dependence on that" means that it arises and is produced as a continuous stream.

Alternatively, in whichever realm (*dhātu*) or stage (*bhūmi*) the *ālayavijñāna* is a maturation (*vipāka*), the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) also belongs to that same realm and stage. Because its activity is bound to that [ālayavijñāna], it relies upon it and takes it as its object; thus, it has the *ālayavijñāna* itself as its object. This is because, through association with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, it conceives "I" and "mine," thereby taking the *ālayavijñāna* as its object. But how can that very mind from which [the afflicted mind] arises also become its own object?

Just as for certain individuals who do not desire it, at a particular stage, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises from that very same [source] from which the mind (*manas*) arises, and it arises having that very thing as its object;

and since the consciousness called "mind" has the name "mind" as its designation, it proceeds depending upon the *ālayavijñāna* and takes that as its object— the term "called mind" distinguishes it from both the *ālayavijñāna* and the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Furthermore, as to what its intrinsic nature is, he says:
"its nature is mentation.
Thus, because its nature is mentation, it is called "manas" according to the rules of etymological derivation (*nairūkta*).
Because its nature is that of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is necessarily associated with mental factors (*caitta*).
However, it is not yet known which mental factors, how many, or for how long it is associated; therefore, he says:
"It is always accompanied by the four afflictions (*kleśa*), which are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). (6ab)
For mental factors (caitta) are of two kinds: afflictions (kleśa) and those other than them.
To distinguish them from the others, he says "by the afflictions" (kleśaiḥ).
Furthermore, the afflictions are sixfold.
And because it does not associate with them, he says "by four.
"Accompanied" (sahita) means associated (saṃprayukta).
Furthermore, the afflictions (kleśa) are also of two kinds.
[They are] unwholesome and obscured-unspecified.
He says "by means of the obscured-unspecified" for the purpose of distinguishing them from the unwholesome;
for it is not possible for there to be an association of unwholesome [states] with an obscured consciousness.
They are "obstructed" because they are afflicted;
they are "indeterminate" because they are not defined as either wholesome or unwholesome;
and they are "always" present at all times.
As long as that exists, it is associated with those [defilements].
Since they are not known specifically due to a general description, he specifies them:
"designated as self-view, self-delusion, self-pride, and self-love" (6cd).
The view that there is a self in the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) is the "view of self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), which means the "view of a real body" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Delusion (*moha*) is ignorance (*ajñāna*);
ignorance regarding the self is "delusion about the self" (*ātmamoha*).

Self-pride (*ātmamāna*) means pride regarding the self; its meaning is the "pride of 'I am'" (*asmimāna*). Self-attachment (*ātmasneha*) means attachment to the self; its meaning is love for the self (*ātmaprema*).
In that regard, being deluded concerning the nature of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), one produces the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) with respect to the storehouse-consciousness.
The inflation of the mind arising from the view of a self is the conceit "I am" (asmimāna).
When these three are present, the attachment toward that object which is regarded as a self is self-love (ātmasneha).
And it is said:
By ignorance, by the view of self, by the conceit "I am," and by craving—
by these four, the mind characterized by mentation is defiled.
But that afflicted mind, which has perversion as its cause, is always present;
it is the constant cause of the notion of "I" even when the mind is wholesome or neutral.
For these afflictions, beginning with self-delusion (*ātmamoha*), like the mind itself, belong to nine levels (*navabhūmika*).

Since they are mentioned here in general terms, it is not known whether they are associated only with those belonging to their own level or also with those belonging to other levels; therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "wherever born, associated with that which consists of it" (*yatrajas tanmayair*): "wherever born" means born in a particular place.
"Consisting of that" means that in whichever realm (*dhātu*) or level (*bhūmi*) one is born, one is associated only with those [mental factors] belonging to that realm and that level.
It is not associated with [afflictions] belonging to other realms or other stages.
Furthermore, is it associated with only the four afflictions? No, he says; it is also associated with others, such as contact (sparśa) and so forth. 7b
"Is associated" (*saṃprayujyate*) means it is conjoined (*saṃbadhyate*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
"By contact and so forth" (*sparśādyaiḥ*) refers to contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).

For these five factors, because they are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*), are associated with all consciousnesses. Furthermore, wherever one is born, one is associated only with those [factors] belonging to that same realm and level (*tanmaya*), and not with those belonging to other realms or levels.
Alternatively, the phrase "or with others" is used for the purpose of distinguishing them from those associated with the root-consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
For in the root-consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), contact and the other [mental factors] are non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
However, in the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), they are obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), just like the mind itself.
If that afflicted mind were to function without distinction throughout the states of wholesome, afflicted, and indeterminate, then it would have no cessation.
And if that [defilement] has not ceased, how can there be liberation? Thus, why would it not follow that liberation is non-existent?
It does not so follow, because that [defilement] does not exist for the Arhat.
Nor does it exist in the attainment of cessation, nor in the supramundane path.
(7bcd) First of all, because an Arhat has abandoned the afflictions without remainder, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) does not exist at all.

For that [afflicted mind] is abandoned precisely by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) upon the attainment of Arhatship, just like the afflictions belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) which are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Like other afflictions (*kleśa*), it does not exist at all in the state of arhatship. Furthermore,

for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) and has attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), [the latent tendency] is suppressed even during the state of the attainment of cessation— just like the Path— because the attainment of cessation is obtained through the power of the Path.
And for one who has emerged from cessation, it proceeds again from the *ālayavijñāna* alone;
[it does not proceed] from the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*).
The inclusion of the term "supramundane" is for the purpose of excluding the mundane.
On the mundane path, however, the afflicted mind continues to function.
Because the vision of selflessness is the antidote to the vision of a self, it cannot endure on the supramundane path;
due to the non-simultaneity of the discordant factor and its antidote, that [afflicted mind] ceases upon the supramundane path.
Therefore, even for one who has emerged from that state, it arises again from the *ālayavijñāna* alone;
this concludes the summary and detailed explanation of the second transformation.
Since the third transformation must be explained immediately after the second transformation, he says:
"The third is that which is the perception of the sixfold object. (8bc)
The third is the transformation of consciousness; this is the completion of the sentence.
"Of the sixfold" means of the six types of objects consisting of form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena (*dharma*); "apprehension" means grasping or comprehension.
Furthermore, as to whether that [apprehension] is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, he says:
"Wholesome, unwholesome, and non-dual" (8d).
"Wholesome, unwholesome, and non-dual" also includes the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
That which is associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion is wholesome.
That which is associated with greed, hatred, and delusion is unwholesome;

that which is not associated with either wholesome or unwholesome factors is "twofold," meaning it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome. Furthermore, with what kind of mental factors (caitasika) is it associated?
Or how many mental factors (caitasika) are associated with it? To this he says:

"It is associated with the universal, the specific, and the wholesome mental factors; likewise with the afflictions (kleśa) and the secondary afflictions (upakleśa); it possesses the three types of feeling. (9)

Since these [factors] mentioned as "pervasive" (sarvatraga) and so forth are not understood, he says the following in order to demonstrate them: "The first are contact and the rest. The meaning is that they are called "pervasive" because they were indicated at the beginning. For instance:
"Always accompanied by contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition" (3cd)—
thus they were first indicated.
Since contact is the first among these, they are called "contact and the rest" (*sparśādayaḥ*).
Furthermore, these five factors—contact, attention, and so forth—accompany every state of mind; thus, they are called "universal" (*sarvatraga*).
For they function without distinction in the *ālayavijñāna*, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
With reference to the "specifically determined" (*viniyata*) factors, he says:
Desire, resolve, and mindfulness, together with concentration and wisdom, are fixed; they are called "fixed" because they are restricted to specific objects. 10bc.
For their object is indeed specific, not universal.
Among these, *chanda* (desire) is the longing for an intended object.
By the phrase "longing for an intended object," its restricted scope is indicated, since there is no desire for what is not intended.
That object which is intended as the domain of activities such as seeing and hearing is the "intended" (*abhipreta*).
In that regard, *chanda* (desire) is the aspiration for seeing, hearing, and so forth;
its function is to provide a basis for the undertaking of vigor (*vīrya*).
Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is the ascertainment of a determined object exactly as it is.
The inclusion of the term "determined" is for the purpose of excluding what is undetermined.
An object that is free from doubt, whether by means of reasoning or through the instruction of a reliable authority, is "determined."

Adhimokṣa (resolute conviction) is the mental fixation upon an object by means of that very aspect—such as the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and so forth—by which it was previously determined; it is the ascertainment that "it is thus and not otherwise. Its function is to be unshakeable.

For one who is preeminent in resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) cannot be diverted from their own tenets by the proponents of other doctrines. Memory (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetfulness of a familiar object and the mind’s capacity for verbal expression regarding it.
A "familiar object" is one previously experienced.
Non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa*) is the cause for not losing the apprehension of the object.
Recollection (*abhilapanatā*) is the repeated recollection of the mode of the object previously apprehended;
"recollection" itself is the state of recollecting (*abhilapanatā*).
Furthermore, it has non-distraction as its function.
Because there is no distraction of the mind toward another object or another aspect when the object is being verbally articulated, it has non-distraction as its function.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the one-pointedness of the mind upon the object to be examined.
The object to be examined is [considered] either in terms of its qualities or its defects.
One-pointedness is the state of having a single focal object.
Its function is to provide a basis for knowledge.
Because of the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are when the mind is concentrated,
*dhī* is wisdom (*prajñā*). This too is the discernment of the very object under investigation, whether it is conducted through proper application or improper application, or otherwise.
"Discernment" (*pravicaya*) means that which discerns;
it is the analytical comprehension of phenomena, whether correctly or incorrectly, as if they were mixed together in their specific and general characteristics.
"Reasoning" (*yukti*) is application (*yoga*).
Furthermore, that authoritative instruction consists of inference and direct perception.
That which is produced by these three modes of application is "established through yoga.
Moreover, it is [threefold]: consisting of hearing, consisting of reflection, and consisting of cultivation.
Among these, the understanding that arises from the authority of the words of a reliable person is that which consists of hearing (*śrutamaya*).

That which is born from reflecting on reasoning is that which consists of reflection (*cintāmaya*). That which is born from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is that which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
Improper application consists of instruction from an unreliable source, fallacious inference, and wrongly directed meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

That which is produced by such improper application is "established through improper application. Furthermore, that which is acquired through natural endowment (*upapattipratilambhika*) and the comprehension of worldly conventions (*laukikavyavahāra*) are neither established through proper application nor established through improper application.
And this [faith] has the function of removing doubt;
for one who discerns phenomena through wisdom, doubt is removed by the attainment of certainty.
Indeed, these five factors also operate even when they are mutually distinct from one another.
And thus, wherever there is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), the others do not necessarily have to be present there;
this should be stated in all cases.
The specific mental factors (*viniyata*) have been explained.
Since the wholesome factors mentioned immediately after those [unwholesome ones] must now be explained, he says:
Faith, then shame, dread of blame, The triad beginning with non-greed, vigor, Tranquility, along with heedfulness. (10d)
Non-violence and the wholesome [states]—these eleven factors are the remainder of the sentence (11abc).
Among these, faith (*śraddhā*) is conviction regarding existence, possession of qualities, and capability; it is clarity of mind and aspiration toward the fruits of karma, the truths, and the jewels.
For faith operates in three ways:
it has the aspect of conviction toward an existing entity, whether it possesses qualities or lacks them;
and it has the aspect of serene clarity toward an existing entity that possesses qualities.
When a virtuous quality is present and capable of being attained or produced, it takes the form of longing; this is the clarity of the mind (*cetasaḥ prasāda*).

For faith (*śraddhā*) is the antithesis of mental turbidity; therefore, through its association, the turbidity of the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) is removed, and the mind becomes clear by resorting to faith. Thus, it is called the "clarity of the mind."
Furthermore, its function is to provide a basis for aspiration (*chanda*).
*Hrī* (moral shame) is the feeling of shame regarding a transgression, having made either oneself or the Dharma the predominant factor.
A transgression (*avadya*) is indeed evil, because it is censured by the virtuous and because it results in an undesirable maturation (*vipāka*).

The dejection of the mind, whether due to a fault committed or not committed, which consists of shame, is *hrī* (moral shame). Its function is to provide a basis for restraint from misconduct. *Apattrāpya* (moral dread) is shame regarding a fault by taking the world as one's authority.
For one feels shame regarding what is blameworthy out of fear for ill-repute and so forth, thinking: "This is indeed censured in the world, and knowing me to be such an actor, they will censure me.
This also has the function of providing a basis for the restraint of misconduct.
Non-greed (*alobha*) is the antidote to greed (*lobha*).

Greed (*lobha*) is attachment to and longing for existence (*bhava*) and the requisites of existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*). Its opposite is non-greed (*alobha*), which is non-attachment to and aversion toward existence and the requisites of existence.
Its function is to provide a basis for the non-engagement in misconduct (*duścarita*).
Non-hatred (*adveṣa*) is the antidote to hatred; it is loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
For hatred is malice toward sentient beings, toward suffering, and toward those things that are the basis of suffering.
Because non-hatred is the antidote to hatred, it is the absence of malice toward sentient beings, toward suffering, and toward those things that are the basis of suffering.
This [non-delusion] also has the function of providing a basis for the non-occurrence of misconduct.
Non-delusion (amoha) is the antidote to delusion (moha); it is the correct realization of things as they truly are.
Delusion is ignorance regarding the results of karma, the [four] truths, and the [three] jewels.

Non-delusion (*amoha*) is the antidote to delusion; it is the correct understanding regarding those very same [objects]: the fruits of action, the [Four] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels. Its function is also to provide a basis for the non-engagement in misconduct. Energy (*vīrya*) is the antidote to laziness (*kausīdya*); it is the mental exertion toward what is wholesome.
But it is not so in the case of the defiled;
for in the defiled state, enthusiasm is indeed laziness because of its contemptible nature.
And this [effort] has the function of fulfilling and perfecting the side of wholesome qualities.
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is the antidote to rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*); it is the serviceability (*karmaṇyatā*) of body and mind.
Rigidity is the unserviceability of body and mind, as well as the seeds of the defiled phenomena (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*).
This is because when that [rigidity] is removed, pliancy truly exists.
In this context, bodily pliancy (*kāyakarmaṇyatā*) is that from which there arises in the body a lightness of movement toward its own functions.

Mental pliancy (*cittakarmaṇyatā*) is a distinct mental factor (*caitasika dharma*) that serves as the cause for joy and lightness in a mind associated with correct attention (*samyag-manasikāra*); because of its connection with this, the mind proceeds toward its object without obstruction, and therefore it is called mental pliancy.
Furthermore, bodily pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) should be understood as a specific quality of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyaviśeṣa*) itself, brought forth by joy (*prīti*).
This is because it is stated in the Sūtra: "The body of one whose mind is joyful becomes pliant.
By virtue of this [joy], through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), its function is the extraction of all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
It is accompanied by heedfulness;
it proceeds together with heedfulness, thus it is "accompanied by heedfulness.
What, then, is this?
It is equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Why is this so?

Because it is exclusively wholesome, because all wholesome factors are the subject of exposition here, because it is not explicitly mentioned like faith and the others, and because there are no other wholesome factors apart from it.
It is understood as equanimity itself.
In that context, heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the antidote to heedlessness (*pramāda*). Heedfulness consists of everything from non-greed up to vigor (*vīrya*).

Those non-attachment and other [wholesome roots] by relying upon which one abandons unwholesome states and cultivates the wholesome states that are their antidotes—those non-attachments and so forth are heedfulness (*apramāda*).
For this very reason, it is the antidote to heedlessness (*pramāda*), because it is the opposite of heedlessness.
Furthermore, its function is the fulfillment of mundane and supramundane success.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is evenness of mind, composure of mind, and effortlessness of mind.
By these three terms, the initial, middle, and final stages of equanimity are illuminated.
In this context, laxity (*laya*) or excitement (*auddhatya*) constitutes an imbalance of the mind.
Due to the absence of that [distraction], there is first equanimity of mind; then,

for one whose mind is concentrated through lack of volitional effort and exertion, that proceeding of the mind exactly as it is, in accordance with the situation, is mental pliancy (*cittapraśrabdhi*).
Furthermore, that state is accompanied by the apprehension of lethargy and excitement because it has not yet been long cultivated.

Then, through the attainment of excellence in cultivation and the distancing of its opposites, when that apprehension no longer exists, there occurs for the mind a state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*)—not applying effort toward the signs that counteract lethargy and excitement.
And this [state] has the function of providing a basis that allows no room for any primary or secondary afflictions.
Non-violence (*avihiṃsā*) is the antidote to violence (*vihiṃsā*).
Non-violence is the absence of harm toward sentient beings through killing, binding, and so forth; it is compassion (*karuṇā*) for sentient beings.
It is called *karuṇā* because it restrains (*ruṇaddhi*) suffering (*kaṃ*).

*Kam* is a designation for happiness; the meaning is that it obstructs suffering. For one who is compassionate (*kāruṇika*) becomes pained by the suffering of others. And this [compassion] has non-harming as its function.
The eleven wholesome [factors] have been explained.
Since the afflictions were mentioned immediately after them, he speaks with reference to them:
"The afflictions are attachment, aversion, and delusion. (11d)
"And pride, views, and doubt" (12a).
Attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and delusion (*mūḍhi*) constitute "attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Among these, attachment is the fixation upon and the longing for existence and enjoyments.
Furthermore, its function is the production of suffering.
Here, "suffering" refers to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*), because they are brought into existence through the power of craving for the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Therefore, the function of attachment is specified as the production of suffering.

Hostility (*pratigha*) is malice toward sentient beings; it is a harshness of mind by which one, being possessed, contemplates harm such as the killing or binding of sentient beings. Its function is to provide a basis for an unpleasant state of existence and for misconduct. "Contact" (*sparśa*) is pleasure.
Abiding together with that is "abiding in comfort" (*sparśavihāra*). Not abiding in comfort is "non-abiding in comfort" (*asparśavihāra*);
the meaning is that it is accompanied by suffering.

Because a mind of malice (*āghātacitta*) inevitably gives rise to mental distress (*daurmanasya*), the mind is tormented; and because the body conforms to the mind, the body too is indeed tormented. Thus, in all postures (*īryāpatha*), one dwells with suffering and affliction, in a state of non-contact (*asparśavihāra*).

Furthermore, for one whose mind is struck down by resentment, no misconduct (*duścarita*) is far off; therefore, resentment is said to have the function of providing a basis for dwelling in non-contact and for misconduct.

Delusion (*moha*) is the ignorance regarding the miserable destinies, the happy destinies, nirvāṇa, the causes that establish one therein, and the non-perverted relationship between cause and fruit for these.
Its function is to provide a basis for the arising of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
In this context, affliction is threefold, consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth.
Its arising (*utpatti*) is the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) by each subsequent defilement (*saṃkleśa*) due to the cause of each preceding defilement.
Its function is to provide a basis for that arising;

for it is only in one who is deluded (*mūḍha*)—and not in one who is not deluded—that there occurs the engagement of false knowledge, doubt, attachment, and other afflictions, as well as the karma leading to rebirth and birth itself.
Pride: indeed, every form of pride arises based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, its characteristic is the inflation of the mind.
For, having superimposed the state of "self" and "mine" upon the aggregates, one elevates the self through various distinctions, thinking, "I am this," or "this is mine."
One considers oneself superior to others;
its function is to provide a basis for disrespect and the arising of suffering.

Disrespect (*agaurava*) is haughtiness toward teachers and virtuous persons, as well as a lack of humility in body and speech. Furthermore, the arising of suffering here refers to the arising of renewed existence (*punarbhava*).

Furthermore, although there is no difference in the essential nature of this mental inflation (*cittonnati*), it is divided into seven types based on the differences in its causes, such as pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and so forth.

Pride is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior" in terms of family, knowledge, wealth, and so on, compared to one who is inferior in family, knowledge, wealth, and so on; or that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am equal" in terms of family and so on, compared to one who is actually equal.
That is pride (*māna*).

Excessive pride (*atimāna*) is as follows: when one who is equal in terms of family, knowledge, wealth, and so forth, thinks "I am superior" in terms of generosity, ethical discipline, prowess, and so forth; or when one who is superior in terms of family, learning, and so forth, thinks "I am equal" in terms of knowledge, wealth, and so forth—this is excessive pride.

The inflation of the mind thinking, "I alone am superior in terms of lineage, knowledge, and wealth" when one is actually superior in lineage, knowledge, and wealth—this is *mānātimāna* (conceit beyond conceit).

*Asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"): the inflation of the mind arising from the attachment to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya*) regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which are devoid of a self or anything belonging to a self—this is *asmimāna*.
*Abhimāna* (conceit): the inflation of the mind thinking, "I have attained it," regarding a higher, specific realization that has not yet been attained—this is *abhimāna*.

Inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*): the inflation of the mind thinking, "I am only slightly inferior in terms of family, learning, and so forth, compared to one who is vastly superior in family, learning, and so forth"—this is inferiority pride.
False pride (*mithyāmāna*):
the inflation of the mind thinking, "I possess qualities" when one actually lacks qualities—this is false pride.
Lack of qualities refers to immorality and the like; one in whom these exist is "one who lacks qualities.

Therefore, by thinking "I am possessed of qualities," one accepts the state of possessing qualities even in the absence of generosity, morality, and so forth. Consequently, because it lacks a real basis, it is called "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*).

Although "view" (*dṛk*) is a general designation, because this occurs in the context of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is connected specifically to the five views consisting of afflictions, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the others.
Neither mundane right view nor the untainted [right view] is included here.
However, although these views are not distinguished by their being afflicted and investigative in nature, they differ from one another due to differences in their objects and aspects.
Among them, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the perception of a self or what belongs to a self within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).

The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the perception of those very five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which have been grasped as self or belonging to a self, as either annihilated or eternal.

False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is that false view by which one denies the cause, the fruit, or action, or destroys an existing reality; it is called "false view" because it is the most sinful of all views.

Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the vision of the five aggregates of clinging as being foremost, superior, excellent, and supreme. Adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is the vision of the five aggregates of clinging as being purification, liberation, and the means to definitive deliverance.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is indecision regarding the results of actions, the [Four] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels.
Doubt (*vimati*) is a wavering mind characterized by the thought "it might be so" or "it might not be so. Furthermore, this has been stated as a distinct category from wisdom (*prajñā*).
The six primary afflictions (*kleśa*) have already been explained; now, the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which were listed immediately after them, must be discussed. Therefore, he says:
Furthermore, there are anger and enmity;
concealment, vexation, envy, and avarice along with deceit;
guile, pride, harmfulness, lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, and restlessness. (12bcd)
Lack of faith, then laziness, heedlessness, and lost mindfulness;
distraction, lack of clear awareness, regret, and even torpor; as well as applied thought and sustained thought—these secondary afflictions belong to the two [categories] and are twofold. (13–14)
In this context, anger (*krodha*) is a state of mental malice (*āghāta*) arising from a present harm;
and because it has the nature of malice, it is not distinct from hostility (*pratigha*).
However, since it is designated as a specific state of that hostility, it is a derivative of hostility.

Hostility (*krodha*) is designated as that mental resentment (*āghāta*) which arises upon experiencing a present injury, directed toward sentient or non-sentient objects, and whose function is to provide a basis for inflicting punishment and so forth.
Enmity (*upanāha*) is the persistence of hostility;
it is the non-relinquishment and continuous continuation of that underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) consisting of enmity, following after anger, with the thought: "This person has done me this injury."
And this [malice] has the function of providing a basis for intolerance (*akṣānti*).
Intolerance is the failure to endure harm and the desire to retaliate.
This too, like anger (*krodha*), is designated within a specific state of hatred.
Therefore, it should be understood as existing only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*).
Concealment (*mrakṣa*) is the hiding of one's own faults.

It is the hiding of faults belonging to the category of delusion (*moha*), occurring when one who desires one's welfare questions one at the proper time—having set aside desire, hatred, fear, and so forth—saying, "You have acted in such a way. This is concealment.
However, concealment (*mrakṣa*) is a derivative of delusion (*moha*), because its mode of activity is that of hiding.
Its function is to provide a basis for remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and for a lack of physical ease (*asparśa*).

This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): for one who conceals a fault, remorse arises; and from remorse, there necessarily follows a state of unease due to association with mental distress (*daurmanasya*). Thus, it results in a dwelling in discomfort (*asparśavihāra*).
*Pradāśa* (maliciousness) is the biting of fierce speech; "fierce speech" refers to intense harshness by way of striking at the vital points. One whose nature is to bite (*daśana*) is a *dāśī*.
The state of being that is "biting" (*dāśitā*).
And this suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used in its own sense (*svārthika*).
One who bites with fierce words is thus called "one who bites with fierce words" (*caṇḍavacodāśitā*).

And since this has the nature of mental resentment preceded by anger and enmity, it is merely a part of *pratigha* (hostility) and does not exist as a separate substance. Furthermore, its function is to produce verbal misconduct and to cause a state of non-harmony, because a person possessing it dwells in suffering due to living with difficulty.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the resentment of the mind toward the prosperity of others.

For one who is attached to gain and honor, envy is a form of hatred consisting of intolerance directed toward the specific qualities of another—such as gain, honor, lineage, ethical conduct, and learning—which one perceives; it is the resentment of the mind produced by that intolerance.
Resentment is so called because it pervades its own basis (*āśraya*).

Because it is associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and because it is preceded by that [distress], resulting in an unpleasant state of being (*asparśavihāra*), it is said to have the function of mental distress and an unpleasant state of being. Avarice (*mātsarya*) is a grasping of the mind that is opposed to giving.

Giving (*dāna*) is that by which an acquired object—consisting of the Dharma, material goods, or skills—is bestowed upon one who asks or one who does not ask, out of a desire to honor or to benefit them.

Because giving is absent when that [miserliness] exists, it is said to be its opposite. Mātsarya (miserliness) is the mind's attachment—a portion of passion—toward the requisites for life in one who is intent upon gain and honor; it is the desire not to relinquish them.
Its function is to provide a basis for non-austerity (*asaṃlekha*).

Furthermore, lack of austerity (*asaṃlekha*) should be understood as the accumulation of requisites, even those not being utilized, due to stinginess (*mātsarya*). Deceit (*māyā*) is the display of unreal things for the purpose of deceiving others;

it is the manifestation of qualities such as ethical discipline (*śīla*) in a manner other than they actually exist, by one who is intent on gain and honor and possesses the intention to deceive others.

And since this [deceit] arises from passion and delusion acting together—being designated when those two are combined—it exists only as a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*) and not as a substantial entity (*dravya*), like anger and other such states.
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) is the crookedness of the mind comprised of the means for concealing one's own faults;
the means for concealing one's own faults is the deluding of others.
Furthermore, by resorting to one thing after another, one distracts [the mind] or proceeds in an unclear manner;
for this very reason, deceit (*śāṭhya*) is distinct from concealment (*mrakṣa*). For the latter conceals [the fault] quite openly, not by means of an indirect intonation (*kāku*); this too [is so].
Driven by attachment and delusion, which are intent upon gain and honor, one engages in concealing one's own faults and deceiving others;
it is designated as the conjunction of these two alone.
Furthermore, its function is to obstruct the attainment of correct instruction.

Pride— which consists of mental exaltation and the total obsession of one who is attached to his own prosperity— creates an obstacle to the attainment of correct instruction and to wise attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
One's own prosperity consists of excellence in family, health, youth, strength, beauty, sovereignty, intelligence, and wisdom.

*Uddharṣa* is a specific kind of joy (*harṣaviśeṣa*). By means of that specific joy, the mind is rendered independent; because it is thereby made subject to itself, it becomes "overwhelmed" (*paryātta*). This is what is meant by the "overwhelming of the mind.
And its function is to provide a basis for all primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*).
Harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) is the injury of sentient beings (*sattvaviheṭhanā*).
Harmfulness is the harming of sentient beings through various means such as killing, binding, beating, and threatening.
It is called the injury of sentient beings because by it sentient beings are injured through the production of suffering and mental distress via killing, binding, and so forth.
Furthermore, that mercilessness which is a part of resentment (*pratigha*), consisting of harshness of mind toward sentient beings and having the function of harming them, is called *vihiṃsā*.
*Āhrīkya* (lack of shame) is the absence of shame regarding one's own faults;
it is the lack of shame regarding a fault even while considering oneself unfit for such an action, and it is the opposite of *hrī* (moral shame).
Lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) is the absence of shame regarding faults in relation to others.

Even for one who understands, "This which I am doing is contrary to the world and the scriptures," that lack of shame regarding such an evil deed is lack of dread of blame, which is the opposite of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
Both of these function as aids to all primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa* and *upakleśa*).

Among the varieties of attachment, aversion, and delusion—which are the causes for the arising of all unwholesome actions—they are designated according to their occurrence, since attachment and aversion do not exist simultaneously; however, they do not exist independently. *Styāna* is the mind’s lack of serviceability, its state of rigidity.
The state of being rigid is *staimitya*; through connection with this, the mind becomes dull and rigid, such that it lacks the capacity to engage with its object.
And this has the function of providing assistance to all primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa* and *upakleśa*).
Because it is designated as a portion of delusion (*moha*), it belongs exclusively to the category of delusion and does not exist separately.
Excitement (*auddhatya*) is the lack of tranquility of the mind.
Tranquility (*vyupaśama*) is indeed *śamatha*; its opposite is non-tranquility (*avyupaśama*).

Furthermore, this [non-tranquility] is the cause of mental non-tranquility for one who recollects former laughter, amusement, play, and so forth that are conducive to passion; its function is to act as an obstacle to *śamatha*.
Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) is the absence of conviction regarding the results of karma, the [Four Noble] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels; it is the antithesis of faith (*śraddhā*).
Faith (śraddhā) is, respectively, conviction, clarity, and aspiration regarding existence, possession of qualities, and capability.
Lack of faith (aśraddhā) is the opposite of that: it is the absence of conviction, lack of clarity, and lack of aspiration regarding existence, possession of qualities, and capability.
Its function is to provide a basis for laziness (kausīdya).
Because one who lacks faith has no desire for application, its function is to provide a basis for laziness (*kausīdya*).
Laziness is the lack of enthusiasm of the mind toward the wholesome; it is the opposite of vigor (*vīrya*).
It is that portion of delusion which, relying on the pleasure of sleep and reclining, consists of the mind’s lack of enthusiasm toward wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
And this [heedlessness] has the function of obstructing application to the side of the wholesome.

Heedlessness consists of those greed, hatred, delusion, and laziness by which one does not protect the mind from afflictions such as passion, hatred, and delusion, nor cultivate the wholesome states that serve as their antidotes;
heedlessness is designated with respect to those instances of greed, hatred, delusion, and laziness.
And this [forgetfulness] has the function of providing a basis for the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states. Lost mindfulness is afflicted mindfulness;
"afflicted" means associated with the defilements (kleśa).
And this [mental factor] has the function of providing a basis for distraction (*vikṣepa*).
Distraction is a portion of attachment, aversion, and delusion; it is the scattering of the mind.
It is called "distraction" because by means of it the mind is scattered in various ways.

Distraction (*vikṣepa*) is designated, as the case may be, with respect to those passions—attachment, aversion, and delusion—by which the mind is cast outward from the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This [distraction] has the function of obstructing dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) is wisdom associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*), by means of which one proceeds in unperceived ways in the conduct of body, speech, and mind during activities such as approaching and departing, due to ignorance regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done.
And this has the function of providing a basis for transgression.
*Kaukṛtya* is mental regret;
it is called *kukṛta* because that which was done is contemptible (*kutsita*).
Its state is *kaukṛtya* (remorse). Here, however, *kaukṛtya* refers to the mental regret (*vilekha*) concerning what has been poorly done, because the context concerns mental factors (*caitasika*).
And this has the function of being an obstacle to the stability of the mind.
Drowsiness (*middha*) is the contraction of the mind whose functioning has become independent.
Functioning (*vṛtti*) is the engagement with an object.
Drowsiness is that from which the independence of the mind arises.
Drowsiness (*middha*) is that from which an independent mental activity arises that is incapable of sustaining the body.

It is a contraction of the mind, characterized by the non-functioning of the sense faculties such as the eye and so forth. Because it is designated as a portion of delusion (*moha*), it belongs to the category of delusion, and its function is to provide a basis for the neglect of duties.
Vitarka is a mental discourse that investigates; it is a specific form of discernment (prajñā) and volition (cetanā).
It is "investigating" because it functions in the mode of examining, [asking] "What is this?
It is "mental discourse" (manojalpa) because it is the speech of the mind.
"Speech" (*jalpa*) is like the act of speaking;
"speech" is the verbal expression of meaning.
It is a specific form of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), because volition consists in the movement of the mind, while wisdom takes the form of discerning between virtues and faults.

Because the mind functions under their influence, *vitarka* (applied thought) is sometimes designated as the mind and volition (*cetanā*), and sometimes as wisdom (*prajñā*) and the mind, respectively, in the states of non-investigation and investigation.
Alternatively, *vitarka* is designated as volition and wisdom themselves, because the mind functions in such a manner under their influence;
it is precisely this that constitutes the grossness of the mind.
Coarseness (*audārikatā*) refers to grossness, because its mode consists in the investigation of mere objects;
this same principle should also be understood to apply to analysis (*vicāra*).
For analysis, too, has as its nature a specific form of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

The investigative [mind] is merely mental discourse (*manojalpa*), because it discerns what was previously attained, thinking, "This is that. For this very reason, it is called the subtlety of mind (*cittasūkṣmatā*).
These two have the function of providing a basis for dwelling in either comfort or discomfort;
they are established as distinct from one another because of their coarse and subtle natures.
Thus it is said: "In each pair, there are two" (14d).
Two pairs [of factors] are in two categories;
these are remorse and torpor, as well as applied thought and sustained thought.
These four factors are of two kinds: defiled and non-defiled.
In that regard, the mental remorse that arises from not having done what is unwholesome and having done what is wholesome is afflicted regret (*kaukṛtya*).
That regret which arises from not having done what is wholesome and having done what is unwholesome is non-afflicted.
Sleep (*middha*) is also afflicted when it is pierced by an afflicted mind and associated with an afflicted mind.
That which is not pierced by an afflicted mind and is associated with an unafflicted mind is unafflicted.
Discursive thoughts (vitarka) such as those of sensual desire, ill-will, and harmfulness are afflicted;
discursive thoughts such as those of renunciation are unafflicted.
Thus, the investigation of means for harming others is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*),
whereas the investigation of means for benefiting others is unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*).

In that regard, only those instances of regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*) that are afflicted are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and not the others.

In that regard, just as the perception of forms, sounds, and so forth—which occurs in six ways according to possibility—is associated with all mental factors (caitasika), namely the universal, the object-specific, the wholesome, the afflictions (kleśa), and the secondary afflictions (upakleśa); likewise, the three types of feeling are associated with the three feelings: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Because it arises in relation to forms and other objects that serve as the bases for mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), mental displeasure (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), [the mental factors] are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
However, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is associated only with the five universal [mental factors] and no others;
and in that case, the feeling (*vedanā*) is exclusively equanimity, and it is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is always associated with the five universal mental factors and with the four afflictions, beginning with self-delusion (*ātmamoha*).
In that state, the feeling is exclusively equanimity (*upekṣā*), and its nature is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This is now considered.

Why is it that, even when the objective conditions for the five [consciousnesses], such as visual consciousness and the rest, are simultaneously present, only one arises from the *ālayavijñāna*—and not two or many—as some maintain?

[They argue that] neither two nor many arise simultaneously because of the absence of multiple simultaneous equivalent-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*); thus, only a single consciousness arises.
Furthermore, a single consciousness is not capable of serving as the immediately preceding condition for many [subsequent consciousnesses],
whether according to a fixed rule or without restriction;
if the conditions for only one are present, then only that one arises.
Thus, since the arising occurs when the conditions for two or many [consciousnesses] are present, he says:
"The emergence of the five consciousnesses within the root-consciousness occurs according to their respective conditions, either simultaneously or not, just as waves arise upon the water. (15)
