"Of the five" refers to the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, together with the mental consciousness that follows them.

Because it is the seed-basis for the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, because they arise from it, and because it takes up birth within the realms of existence (*gati*), the *ālayavijñāna* is called the "root-consciousness.
"Arising according to conditions" means that whichever condition for whichever [consciousness] is present, that [consciousness] necessarily arises and attains its own-being.
"Simultaneously or not" means either at once or in succession.

"As waves [arise] from water" is the illustration for the simultaneous or non-simultaneous arising of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). As it has been said:
"For example, Viśālamati, if there is a great flood of water flowing and [someone were to... one wave... [and so forth].
When the condition for the arising of a wave has presented itself, only a single wave proceeds; likewise,
if there are two, three, or many [conditions], [many waves proceed].
When the conditions for the arising of waves are present,
many waves proceed;
yet there is no [cessation] of that torrent of water by its own current.
There is a complete cutting off of what carries [the karmic seeds],
and no further utilization is perceived.
In the very same way, Viśālamati, depending upon the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which stands in the place of that flood, [this occurs].
Having established itself, if the condition for the arising of a single visual consciousness is present, then only a single visual consciousness proceeds;
if the conditions for the arising of two, three, or even five consciousnesses are present, [then those proceed].
It is present as long as the five [consciousnesses] continue to function.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The appropriating consciousness is profound and subtle; like a torrential flood, it proceeds containing all seeds.

This [doctrine] has not been revealed by me to the foolish, lest they should falsely imagine it to be a self (*ātman*). For the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is not accepted as being restricted to each specific consciousness in the same way that the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is;
for it is admitted that every consciousness serves as the immediately preceding condition for the arising of all consciousnesses.

Therefore, even from a single immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the arising of two or many consciousnesses is not contradictory provided that the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is present.

Furthermore, what is the reason here that, in the absence of a restriction regarding the immediately preceding condition, when the objective conditions for all five [sense-consciousnesses] are simultaneously present, only one [consciousness] should arise and not all five?
Therefore, it must be admitted that when an object exists, all five [consciousnesses] arise.
This must now be addressed:
does mental consciousness (manovijñāna) operate simultaneously with the visual and other sensory consciousnesses, or without them?
To the question "Or rather not? he says:

The arising of mental consciousness occurs at all times, except for those in the state of non-perception (asaṃjñika), the two meditative attainments (samāpatti), torpor (middha), and unconsciousness (mūrcchana) which are without mind. (16)
Thus: "at all times" means at every moment, whether together with or without the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth;
he now begins this exception to that general rule:
"except for the state of non-perception."
"From the two attainments, from torpor, and also from the mindless fainting state.
(16bd) Among these, the *asaṃjñika* is the cessation of mental states and mental factors for one who has been reborn among the gods who are non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñisattva*).
The "two attainments" are the attainment of non-conceptuality (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Therein, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) is defined as the cessation of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta*), occurring through a mental attention preceded by the perception of liberation, in one who is free from passion for the third dhyāna but not yet free from passion for the stages above it. This is what is called the attainment of non-perception here.
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) means that by which [something] is ceased.
Furthermore, it is the cessation of the active manifestation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) together with its associated factors (*sasaṃprayoga*),
which is a particular state of the basis (*āśraya*).

And because one attains a basis that is incompatible with the arising of another moment of consciousness immediately after the mind of attainment, it is called a "meditative attainment" (*samāpatti*).

The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—for one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*)—is designated as a specific state of the basis through a mental attention preceded by the perception of a peaceful dwelling; it consists of the mental consciousness together with its associated factors and the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), and like the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), it is conceptually constructed upon this particular state of the basis.

Mindless sleep is called "without mind" because, due to the basis [the body] being overcome by intense drowsiness, the mental consciousness does not function for that duration. Fainting is also without mind;
it is a state where the basis becomes impaired either by an external injury or by an imbalance of wind, bile, and phlegm.
In those states where the activity of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is opposed, one conventionally designates them as "mindless" (*acittika*), such as fainting.
Excluding these five states, it should be understood that the activity of the mental consciousness occurs in all other states.

Thus, when the mental consciousness has ceased in the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) and so forth, from what does it arise again upon its departure, given that death does not occur for one in those states?
Furthermore, that [transformation] arises precisely from the *ālayavijñāna*,
for it contains the seeds of all consciousnesses.
Having indicated that "the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of self and phenomena occurs within that transformation of consciousness," he then explains its threefold nature in detail.

Now, in order to establish the thesis that the metaphorical designation of self and phenomena which occurs is nothing but the transformation of consciousness (*vijñānapariṇāma*), and that neither self nor phenomena exist apart from the transformation of consciousness, he says:
"This transformation of consciousness is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); that which is conceptually constructed [does not exist]."
"Therefore that does not exist; thus all this is representation-only" (verse 17).
This threefold transformation of consciousness that was just described is *vikalpa* (conceptual construction).
The mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms, which take on the forms of superimposed objects, are called *vikalpa*. As it has been said:

Unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), however, consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms. By means of that threefold conceptualization—which has the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*), and the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) together with their associated mental factors—that which is conceptualized as the receptacle-world, the self, the aggregates, the elements, the sense-fields, and objects such as form and sound does not exist. Therefore, this transformation of consciousness is called "conceptualization."
Because it has a non-existent object.
How, then, is it known that its object is non-existent?
For when the cause of something is complete and unimpeded, that thing arises; otherwise, it does not.
Furthermore, consciousness arises even when its objective support (*ālambana*) is non-existent, as in the case of illusions, cities of Gandharvas, dreams, and visual disorders like *timira*.
If the arising of consciousness were dependent upon an objective support, then consciousness would not arise in relation to illusions and the like due to the absence of an object;
therefore, consciousness arises from a preceding, ceased consciousness of a similar kind.
It does not arise from an external object, because it occurs even when that [object] is absent;
furthermore, a mutually contradictory cognition is observed among cognizers even with respect to an undifferentiated object,
and it is not logical for a single thing to possess multiple mutually contradictory natures.
Therefore, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has a superimposed form, its objective support (*ālambana*) must be understood as non-existent.
Having thus avoided the extreme of reification (*samāropānta*), he says, with the desire to avoid the extreme of denial (*apavādānta*):
"Therefore, all this is representation-only" (17cd).
Thus: "by that" means "for that reason.

Because that which is conceptualized by a conceptualization consisting of transformation does not exist by virtue of that [conceptualization], therefore, due to the absence of an object, everything is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
"Everything" refers to the three realms and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The word *mātra* (only) serves to exclude objects beyond that [representation].
The letter *ka* is for the purpose of completing the meter.

If everything is indeed representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and there exists no agent or instrument other than that, how is it that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) proceed from the root-consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) when it is uncontrolled and in the absence of an instrument?
For consciousness contains all seeds; its transformation proceeds in such and such a way through mutual influence, whereby this or that conceptual construction arises.
In this context, because it is accompanied by the capacity to produce all phenomena, consciousness containing all seeds is the *ālayavijñāna*.
For since there is even a consciousness that does not possess all seeds, he says "possessing all seeds" [to specify this one].
He says "consciousness" because some imagine that even something other than consciousness, such as *pradhāna* and so forth, possesses all seeds.
Alternatively:
This fault does not apply, because we observe the relationship of qualifier and qualified even when there is a deviation involving only one term.
"Transformation proceeds in such and such a way through mutual influence" (18bc):
transformation is the becoming otherwise than its previous state.
The meaning of "in such and such a way" is that it reaches a state capable of producing each respective conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) immediately thereafter.

Regarding the phrase "by mutual influence": for instance, when the visual consciousness and the others are engaged in nourishing their own capacities, they become the cause for a transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) characterized by those specific capacities; and that transformation of the storehouse consciousness, in turn, [becomes the cause] for the visual consciousness and the others.
This is the sign.
Thus, because both proceed through mutual influence, various kinds of conceptualization arise from that storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) when it is not presided over by anything else.
Furthermore, regarding the present life, it has already been explained how the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise from the storehouse-consciousness.

Now, demonstrating how future birth is linked when the present birth has ceased within the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), he says: "The latent impressions of karma, together with the impressions of the two-fold grasping, produce another maturation once the previous maturation has been exhausted. (19)
Thus, volition that is meritorious, non-meritorious, or imperturbable is karma.
The capacity deposited in the *ālayavijñāna* by that karma for the sake of producing a future personal existence is the "karmic impression" (*karmavāsanā*).
The "twofold grasping" consists of the grasping of the object (*grāhya-grāha*) and the grasping of the subject (*grāhaka-grāha*).

In this context, the "grasping at the object" (*grāhyagrāha*) is the determination that there exists an object of apprehension distinct from consciousness itself, which is superimposed upon one's own continuum.
The "grasping at the subject" (*grāhakagrāha*) is the certainty that this object is perceived, cognized, and grasped by that consciousness.

The "habitual tendency of the two graspings" (*grāhadvayavāsanā*) is the seed for the future arising of similar objects and subjects of apprehension, projected by the previously arisen grasping at the object and the grasping at the subject.

In this regard, the differentiation of personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) according to the distinction of destinies (*gati*) arises from the distinction of karmic latencies (*karmavāsanā*), just as the differentiation of sprouts arises from the differentiation of seeds.

However, the latency of the two types of grasping (*grāhadvaya-vāsanā*) functions as a cooperative condition for all karmic latencies as they proceed toward the production of the personal existences projected by themselves;
it is just as water and other factors act upon a seed in the production of a sprout.
And thus it is stated that the latencies of karma do not produce maturation unless they are assisted by the latencies of the two-fold grasping;
for this very reason, he says:
"together with the latency of the two-fold grasping."

"When the previous maturation is exhausted, they produce another maturation" (19cd). When that maturation which has been brought about by karma accumulated in a previous birth is exhausted— meaning, at the time of its projection when it remains in its final state— the karmic latencies, together with the latencies of the two types of grasping, [produce another] from the maturation already experienced, according to their strength.
They produce that very storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as another maturation (vipāka),
because there is no other maturation apart from the storehouse consciousness.
By the phrase "when the previous maturation has been exhausted," he avoids the extreme of eternalism (śāśvata-anta).
To claim that [the consciousness] produces another ripening is the extreme of annihilationism.

How is it known that there exists an *ālayavijñāna* distinct from the visual and other sensory consciousnesses, and that this alone— rather than the visual and other sensory consciousnesses— is the possessor of all seeds?
This is established through both scripture and reasoning.
For it has been said by the Blessed One in the Abhidharma-sūtra:
"The element is beginningless and is the common support of all phenomena."
When that exists, all states of existence as well as the attainment of nirvana exist.
Furthermore, neither the progression nor the cessation of saṃsāra is tenable without the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
In this context, the progression of saṃsāra refers to the linking of rebirth (pratisandhibandha) within various classes of beings (nikāyasabhāga);
cessation refers to the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder and the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
In this regard, it is not tenable for consciousness conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) to be anything other than the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
In the absence of consciousness conditioned by formative forces, there would also be an absence of the active process (*pravṛtti*).

If the storehouse consciousness were not accepted, one would have to postulate either the consciousness at rebirth (*pratisandhi-vijñāna*) as being conditioned by formative forces, or the six groups of consciousness as being permeated by formative forces.

In that regard, since those formations (*saṃskāra*) which are intended to be the condition for the consciousness at rebirth have long since ceased, and because what has ceased is non-existent, and what is non-existent lacks the status of being a condition, it is not logical that the consciousness at rebirth has formations as its condition.
Furthermore, at the moment of rebirth, there is both name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and not merely consciousness alone.
In that regard, what is the reasoning for [claiming] that consciousness alone is conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and not name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)?
Therefore, it should be stated that name-and-form is conditioned by formative forces,
but not consciousness.
[Tvbh_118] What is this other name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that has consciousness as its condition?

If it is argued that it is that which exists at a later time, then what is the specific excellence of that [later name-and-form] over the name-and-form at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhika*), such that only the latter has consciousness as its condition and the former does not; and such that the former has formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its condition and the latter does not?
Therefore, let name-and-form itself have conditioned formations as its condition; what is the use of postulating a separate member such as rebirth-linking consciousness?
Consequently, it is not logical for rebirth-linking consciousness to have conditioned formations as its condition.
Furthermore, even if the six groups of consciousness are permeated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*), it is not logical for consciousness to have formative forces as its condition.
Why?

Because consciousness is not capable of depositing either the latencies of maturation (*vipāka-vāsanā*) or the latencies of outflow (*niṣyanda-vāsanā*) within itself, due to the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
Nor does it exist in the future, because at that time [the object] has not yet arisen, and what has not arisen is non-existent;
nor does it exist in the present, because at that time the former [moment] has already ceased.

Furthermore, in mindless states such as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) conditioned by consciousness would not exist, because it is impossible for a mind permeated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) to arise again.
Due to the absence of that [name-and-form], the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) would not exist;
and so on, up to old age and death conditioned by birth, which would likewise not exist.
Consequently, the very process of cyclic existence would not occur.

Therefore, the formative forces (saṃskāra) have ignorance as their condition, and the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is perfumed by them, is the consciousness that has the formative forces as its condition.
With that as its condition, there is name-and-form (nāmarūpa) at the moment of rebirth; this alone is the faultless principle.
Even the cessation of saṃsāra is not tenable if the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) does not exist.
For the causes of saṃsāra are karma and the afflictions (kleśa), and between these two, the afflictions are primary.
This is because, through the predominance of the afflictions, karma becomes capable of projecting rebirth, and not otherwise.
Likewise, although rebirth has been projected, that rebirth occurs only through the predominance of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), and not otherwise.
Thus, because the afflictions alone are the primary cause for the progression of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), they are its root.
Therefore, when these are abandoned, cyclic existence ceases, and not otherwise.
And the abandonment of that [affliction] is not tenable without the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
How, moreover, is it not tenable? Is the affliction abandoned when it is manifest, or when it exists in the state of its seed?
In that case, the claim that [an affliction] is abandoned only when it has become manifest is indeed undesirable.
For, because one abides in the path of its abandonment, even that which exists in the state of a seed is not abandoned;
for at that time, nothing other than the antidote itself is admitted to exist wherein the seed of the affliction resides and could be abandoned by that antidote.
Now, if it is maintained that the very mind of the antidote is still accompanied by the seeds of the afflictions,
then that which is indeed accompanied by the seeds of the afflictions cannot logically serve as their antidote.
Furthermore, for those whose seeds of the afflictions have not been abandoned, the cessation of saṃsāra is impossible.

Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is permeated by the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*) co-arising with other consciousnesses, through the implantation of nourishment for their own seeds. Furthermore, as for those afflictions and secondary afflictions which arise from the mind itself— due to a specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*) when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) obtain their functional activity according to their strength— their seed, which resides in the storehouse consciousness, is removed by the path that serves as the antidote to those afflictions, which arises simultaneously [with that seed].
When that [defilement] has been removed, defilements no longer arise by means of that basis; thus, the *nirvāṇadhātu* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) is attained.
Furthermore, when the birth projected by previous karma ceases and no further birth is linked to it, the *nirvāṇadhātu* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) is attained.
For even though karma exists, once the defilements have been abandoned, it is incapable of producing rebirth due to the absence of its auxiliary cause.

Thus, since the progression and cessation of saṃsāra occur only when the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) exists and not otherwise, one must necessarily admit that the storehouse consciousness is distinct from the visual and other sensory consciousnesses, and that it alone— not the visual and other sensory consciousnesses— is accompanied by the seeds of all phenomena. A detailed investigation, however, should be understood from the *Pañcaskandhakopanibandha*.
If this is indeed representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), how is there no contradiction with the Sūtras?
For in the Sūtras, three natures (*svabhāva*) are taught: the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*).
There is no contradiction.
Since the three natures are established precisely when there is representation-only (vijñaptimātra),
[the author] asks "How so? and therefore says:

"By whichever conceptualization whatever object is conceptualized, that is merely the imagined nature; it does not exist. (20) Demonstrating the infinity of conceptualizations through the distinction between internal and external objects of conceptualization, he says:
"By whichever conceptualization"—
whatever object is imagined,
whether internal or external, even down to the qualities of a Buddha.
"This is indeed the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva)";
regarding this, he states the reason:
"it does not exist."
Since that object which is the domain of conceptual construction does not exist because it lacks intrinsic being,
that object is therefore of a purely imagined nature;
it does not have a nature dependent upon causes and conditions.
For indeed, it is observed that with respect to a single entity and its absence, there occurs the activity of multiple mutually contradictory conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Yet, it is not tenable for that single entity or its absence to possess multiple mutually contradictory intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, all this is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), because the object thereof has a purely imagined nature (*parikalpitarūpa*).
And it is said in the Sūtra:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, phenomena do not exist in the way that foolish ordinary people are attached to them.
Immediately after the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) must be explained; therefore, he says:
The dependent nature, however, is conceptual construction arising from conditions (21ab).
Here, by the term "conceptual construction," he states the essential nature of the dependent;
and by the phrase "arising from conditions," [he indicates its origin].
He states the basis for the application of the designation "dependent" (*paratantra*):

therein, "imagined construction" (*parikalpa*) refers to the minds and mental factors belonging to the three realms, which are divided into the categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
As it has been said:
Unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), however, consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms.
It is called "dependent" (*paratantra*) because it is governed by other causes and conditions; the meaning is that it is produced [in dependence].
This amounts to saying that its acquisition of self-nature is contingent upon causes and conditions other than itself.
The dependent nature has been explained.
As for how the perfected nature is so called, he says:
"The perfected [nature] is its perpetual absence of that former [nature]. (21cd)

It is "perfected" (pariniṣpanna) by virtue of being perfected through the absence of change. "Of that" refers to the dependent nature (paratantra); "by the former" refers to the imagined (parikalpita). Within that conceptual construction (vikalpa), the state of being grasped and grasper is imagined.
For it is said to be "imagined" because, within that conceptual construction, the status of grasped and grasper is merely imagined despite being non-existent.
That which is the absolute absence, at all times and for all eternity, of that subject-object duality within the dependent nature, is the perfected nature.
Therefore, it is neither different nor non-different from the dependent nature.

(22ab) For this very reason, "it is not" means that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is the perpetual absence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra*). And this state of being devoid [of the imagined] is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
And that *dharmatā* is neither different from nor non-different from the phenomena (*dharma*).

Since the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is the *dharmatā* of the dependent nature (*paratantra*), it should be understood that the perfected is neither different from nor non-different from the dependent.
For if the perfected were different from the dependent, then the dependent would not be empty of the imagined (*parikalpita*).

Furthermore, if it were non-different [from the perfected nature], then even the perfected nature would not have purity as its object, because— like the dependent nature— it would consist of affliction. Likewise, the dependent nature would not consist of affliction,
because— like the perfected nature— it would be non-different from the perfected nature.
It should be stated—as with impermanence and so forth—that it is neither different nor non-different; this is the completion of the sentence.
For it is just like impermanence, suffering, and selflessness.
It is neither different from nor non-different from the conditioned factors and so forth;
for if impermanence were different from the conditioned factors, [it would follow that the conditioned factors are eternal].
In that case, conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) would be eternal.
Alternatively, if they were non-different [from impermanence], then likewise conditioned phenomena would consist of the absence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva), just like impermanence itself.
The same should be said regarding suffering and the other characteristics as well.

If the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is devoid of the state of grasped object and grasping subject, how is it apprehended? Or, if it is not apprehended, how is it known to exist? To this he says:
"When this is not seen, that is not seen" (22d).
"When this is not seen" refers to the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva); "that is not seen" refers to the dependent nature.

When the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is visible to supramundane non-conceptual gnosis, is not seen, not penetrated, and not realized, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is not apprehended by another cognition because it is accessible only to the pure mundane gnosis obtained subsequent to that [supramundane realization]. Therefore, when the perfected nature is not seen, the dependent nature is not seen.
Furthermore, it is not the case that they are not seen even by the knowledge obtained subsequent to supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*).
Thus, it is stated in the *Nirvikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*:

"By means of the knowledge obtained subsequent to that [supramundane knowledge], one realizes all phenomena to be like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, an echo, the moon reflected in water, and a magical creation."
And here, "dharmas" refers to those comprised within the dependent nature (paratantra);
the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna) is of a single flavor like space;
and "knowledge" is as previously described.
One perceives all those phenomena through non-conceptual gnosis by way of their equality with space, because one sees only the suchness of dependent phenomena.

If the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is indeed a substantial entity (*dravya*), how is it that in the Sūtra all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are taught to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), unarisen, and unceasing?
There is no contradiction,
because there is a threefold absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) corresponding to the threefold intrinsic nature.
Having intended [this], the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena was taught.
The specification of the number is for the purpose of making it known that there are exactly three natures and no fourth.
A "nature" (*svabhāva*) is so called because it exists as if by its own respective characteristic.

There are three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*): the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), and the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
All phenomena consist of the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures.
Now, demonstrating which lack of intrinsic nature belongs to each of these three natures, he says:
The first is devoid of intrinsic nature by its very definition;
furthermore, the other is the absence of intrinsic nature because it does not exist through itself.
Since that is the ultimate reality of phenomena, it is also suchness. (24–25ab)

This first, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), is without intrinsic nature by its very definition, because its defining characteristic is merely a mental construction. For example, "form" is defined by the characteristic of form;
"feeling" is defined by the characteristic of experience, and so forth.
And therefore, because it lacks an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), like a flower in the sky, it is devoid of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) by its very essence.
"The other," moreover, refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
It does not have an existence of its own (*na svayaṃbhāvaḥ*), because, like an illusion, it arises through conditions external to itself (*parapratyayena*).
And therefore, since its arising does not exist in the manner that it appears, it is said that its "arising is without intrinsic nature" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and that is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of phenomena, because it is such":
for the supreme is supramundane gnosis (*lokottara-jñāna*) because it is unsurpassed; its object (*artha*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Alternatively, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is called the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) because it is of a single flavor everywhere like space, and because it is characterized by purity and immutability.

Since that perfected nature is the ultimate reality of all phenomena—which are of a dependent nature (*paratantra-ātmaka*)—it is considered their true nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the perfected nature itself is the "lack of intrinsic nature in the sense of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), because the perfected nature has the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāvatva*).
But must the perfected nature be expressed only by the term "ultimate reality"?
No, he says; rather, it is also suchness.
Because of the word "also," it is not to be designated solely by the term *tathatā*;
rather, it is to be designated by as many synonyms for the *dharmadhātu* as there may be.

It is called *tathatā* (suchness) because it exists as such at all times. For it remains exactly as it is at all times throughout the stages of ordinary beings, those in training, and those beyond training;
since it does not become otherwise, it is termed "suchness."

But is the state of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā) identical to suchness (tathatā), which is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna), or is it something else? To this he says: "That very [suchness] is representation-only. (25d)
As it has been said: "Because of the awakening to the perfectly pure characteristic, that mind abides in the name, for at that time one sees only that [name].
And from abiding in the name, the apprehension of representation is abandoned."
Then, through the sequence of cultivation, one touches that realm which is non-apprehension;
at that time, one attains mastery, which is liberation from all obscurations.
Thus, by this statement, "that very [state] is representation-only," the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is expressed.
If all this is indeed representation-only, why does one perceive forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind? To address this question, he says:
"As long as consciousness does not abide in the state of representation-only..."
The latent tendencies of the two types of grasping do not cease for that long.
Alternatively, those karmic impressions, accompanied by the impressions of the two types of grasping, produce another maturation once the previous maturation has been exhausted. (19cd)
Therefore, it has been asked: "How then is there abandonment and non-abandonment? To this he says:
"As long as consciousness does not abide in the state of representation-only," and so forth.
As long as consciousness does not abide in the true nature of mind—which is designated as "representation-only"—but instead operates within the perception of a grasped object and a grasping subject;
that is, the twofold grasping consisting of the grasping of the object and the grasping of the subject;
its latent tendency is the seed deposited therein in the *ālayavijñāna* for the future arising of the twofold grasping.

The meaning is that as long as the yogin’s mind is not established in the state of representation-only (vijñaptimātratva), which is characterized by non-duality, so long does the latent tendency toward the grasped and the grasper (grāhyagrāhakānuśaya) not cease and is not abandoned.
Furthermore, in this context, by the non-abandonment of external perception, the non-abandonment of internal perception is demonstrated;
therefore, the thought occurs to him: "I grasp forms and so forth by means of the eye and other [faculties]."
This must now be explained: does one abide in the true nature of mind (*cittadharmatā*) by perceiving only the mind devoid of objects?
No, he says;
rather, it is because of the perception that "this is indeed representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
"Placing something before him, he does not abide in that alone.
(27cd) Alternatively, there may be one who is conceited and, by mere hearing, thinks, "I am established in pure representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). To eliminate that grasping, it is said:
"For even 'this is representation-only' is [based on] apprehension. (27ab)

"Beginning with: 'This is representation-only (vijñaptimātra), devoid of objects; there is no external object'—thus, by way of apprehension, grasping, and mental elaboration, he places it 'before him,' meaning directly in front. According to what has been heard, because the objects of the yoga-practitioner (yogācāra) are manifold, he says 'something,' such as a skeleton, or a livid corpse, or a festering corpse, or a worm-infested corpse, or a bloated corpse, and so forth; yet he does not abide in that alone."
Because the apprehension of consciousness has not been abandoned.
But when is there the abandonment of the grasping at consciousness, and when does one become established in the true nature of the mind and phenomena? To this he says:
"But when knowledge no longer perceives an object, then..."

Established in the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratva*), because there is no object to be grasped, there is no grasping of that [object]. (28) At whatever time the cognition— whether it has the teaching as its object, the instruction as its object, or ordinary objects such as forms and sounds— does not perceive, does not see, does not grasp, and does not adhere to anything external to the mind, due to seeing the object as it truly is;
But it is not like one born blind; at that time, there is the abandonment of the grasping of consciousness, and one becomes established in the true nature (*dharmatā*) of one's own mind.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "Because, in the absence of an object to be grasped, there is no grasping of that [subject]. (28d)
When there is an object of apprehension, there is an apprehending subject, but not when there is an absence of an object of apprehension.
When there is an absence of an object of apprehension, one realizes the absence of the apprehending subject as well,
and not merely the absence of the object of apprehension.
In this way, non-conceptual supramundane cognition arises in which the object of cognition and the cognizer are exactly equal.
The latent tendencies of attachment to the grasped and the grasper are abandoned, and the mind becomes established in the true nature (*dharmatā*) of its own mind.
When the mind is thus established in representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), how is it designated? To this he says:
It is without mind and without apprehension; it is supramundane gnosis.
It is the revolution of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) through the abandonment of the two kinds of corruption (dauṣṭhulya).
That itself is the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu), inconceivable, wholesome, and eternal.
"This is the blissful body of liberation; this is the so-called Dharma-body of the Great Sage.

(30) Thus, by these two verses, the perfection of the fruit is elucidated for the yogin who has entered into representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), beginning from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and proceeding through subsequent stages of excellence. In that state, because there is no perceiving mind (*grāhakacitta*), there is the non-apprehension of the perceived object (*grāhyārtha*).
It is without thought and non-apprehensible;
because it is not practiced in the world, because it lacks worldly activity, and because it is non-conceptual, it transcends the world, and thus that knowledge is supramundane. (29ab)
In order to indicate that the transformation of the basis occurs immediately after that knowledge, it says:
"the transformation of the basis" (29c).
Here, the "basis" refers to the *ālayavijñāna* which contains all seeds.

Its revolution (*parāvṛtti*) occurs when, through the cessation of the existence of the latencies of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*), maturation, and the two [grasping] (*dvaya-vāsanā*), there is a revolution into the state of flexibility (*karmanya-tā*) and non-dual gnosis (*advaya-jñāna*) as the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
Furthermore, by the abandonment of what is this revolution of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained? To this he says:
"By the twofold abandonment of corruption" (29d).
"Of two kinds" refers to the corruption of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa-dauṣṭhulya*) and the corruption of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa-dauṣṭhulya*).
Corruption is the unserviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*) of the basis;
furthermore, it is the seed (*bīja*) of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations.

Furthermore, that transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is attained through the abandonment of the dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) pertaining to the Śrāvakas and others, which is why it is called the "body of liberation" (*vimuktikāya*); and it is attained through the abandonment of the dysfunctions pertaining to the Bodhisattvas, which is why it is said, "This is the body of the Dharma of the Great Sage. (30d)
The revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is said to be twofold according to the distinction of the obscurations: that which is surpassable and that which is unsurpassable.
On this point, there is a verse:
"The appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*) should be known as characterized by the two obscurations."
It contains all seeds and is the seed of afflictions; therein lies the bondage of both [aspects] for each of the two.
Thus: "of the two" refers to the Śrāvaka and the Bodhisattva.

For the former, it is the seed of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and for the latter, it is the seed of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*); through their eradication, the attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) occurs.
That itself is the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). (30a)
That very [state], which consists of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*),
is called the "outflow-free realm" (*anāsravo dhātu*) because it is free from corruption (*nirdauṣṭhulya*).
It is "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) because it is devoid of all outflows (*sarvāsravavigata*).
It is called a *dhātu* because it is the cause of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*); for here the word *dhātu* has the meaning of "cause.
It is inconceivable because it is beyond the scope of reasoning, because it is to be personally realized within oneself, and because there is no illustrative example [for it].
It is wholesome because its object is pure, because it is secure, and because it consists of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
It is stable because it is eternal due to its inexhaustibility.
It is blissful precisely because it is eternal; for that which is impermanent is suffering, and since this is eternal, it is therefore blissful.
Due to the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the śrāvakas possess the body of liberation (*vimuktikāya*).

That very same [body], characterized by the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), is also called the "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) of the Great Sage, because of his abandonment of both the obscurations of affliction and the knowable (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*) through the cultivation of the stages (*bhūmi*) and perfections (*pāramitā*).
Because of the full realization of the revolution of the basis, it is called the Dharma-body of the Great Sage.

It is called the *dharmakāya* because of the non-abandonment of *saṃsāra*, because of the absence of affliction therein for the Bodhisattvas, and because of the attainment of mastery over all phenomena.
"Of the Great Sage" (*mahāmuni*) refers to the Blessed Buddha as the Great Sage due to his union with supreme silence (*mauna*).
The Commentary on the *Triṃśikāvijñapti* is completed.
The work of the teacher Sthiramati.
